newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protest, far-right voters hold key to French poll.
newsitem.headline: Protest, far-right voters hold key to French poll.

text.p: Voters who abstained in protest or who backed the far right in the first round of France's parliamentary election hold the key to Sunday's cliffhanger runoff ballot.

Political commentators said Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could avoid "cohabitation", or power-sharing with a left-wing prime minister, only by winning over a large slice of those who deserted the ruling centre-right coalition when the Socialist-Communist bloc grabbed an upset victory a week ago.

Within the space of just a few days, Chirac has buried his unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe and fielded socially-conscious Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin in a "dream ticket" attempt to salvage the coalition.

"The Seguin-Madelin ticket has come pretty late. It blurs the outlook because there has never been a change of leader (Prime Minister Alain Juppe) between the two rounds of an election," political commentator Pascal Perrineau told France Info radio.

"The results of the first round show that the centre-right does have some reserves in the contingent which abstained. But that won't be enough. It must capture a majority of those who abstained and an important slice of voters who backed the far-right National Front," Perrineau said.

Centre-right leaders are openly betting on a favourable swing of far-right voters despite Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose party took 15 percent of the vote, urging voters to "punish" the coalition.

Le Pen featured prominently in French newspapers, which pictured him -- eyes popping and mouth wide open as he yelled in rage -- thrusting towards a female Socialist candidate shortly before he threw her to the ground in a campaign brawl in a Paris suburb on Friday.

Across the country, 80 of the 577 parliamentary constituencies are too close to call with less than two percentage points separating candidates in the first round, when the combined left polled 40.1 percent to 36.5 for the centre-right.

On Saturday evening, rugby fans watching the Rugby Union final will be treated to a picture of their country's likely future -- "cohabitation", or power-sharing. In the VIP stand at the stadium will be Chirac, Seguin and Jospin.

If Jospin wins, the Gaullist president is likely to be a lame duck in cohabitation with a hostile government bent on overturning austerity policies geared to fulfilling the criteria for the European single currency.
Seguin, likely premier if the right wins, has warned voters that cohabitation would be as tough as a rugby match.
An increasingly confident Jospin said on Friday: "I ask French men and women...to confirm and amplify the first-round vote."
The conservatives appealed to voters not to let "the trap slam shut" and think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity.

The popular newspaper France-Soir, following a lead set by other dailies, flouted on Saturday a law banning the publishing of opinion polls in the week ahead of elections. It printed six surveys carried out over the past week.
Together with the dailies Le Parisien and the southwest regional newspaper La Republique des Pyrenees, France-Soir runs the risk of a 500,000 franc ($88,000) fine.

Dismissing the law as imbecile and outdated, France-Soir news editor Bernard Morrot invoked the republican right to equality given the fact that such surveys are common knowledge among the Paris establishment.
The anti-surveys law is meant to avoid swaying France's 38.5 million voters. The polls, or rumours of them, are a major factor moving the Paris stock market ahead of the election.

Violence marred the eve of voting, with a bomb exploding outside a post office in the southern port city of Marseille overnight. Police said the bomb late on Friday night caused damage but no casualties.
Investigators did not rule out the possibility the bomb was planted by the Historic Wing of the Corsican National Liberation Front.
